title: Playing with Miles Davis in Buffalo
summary: Herbie Hancock called him for a Miles gig; after a rehearsal at Miles's brownstone, Miles tested him on stage in Buffalo.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Beautiful. Just to wrap up, an acquaintance knew I was going to be talking to you and he said, “Oh he’s played with everyone. I’m curious if he ever recorded with Miles Davis?”

No. I didn’t record with Miles Davis, but I had an episode with Miles Davis. Herbie Hancock called me — well what’s that, my first recording we discussed before, with Grachan Moncur featuring Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams. This is how I met Herbie and those guys. And so apparently I was rather impressive with my dynamic. Herbie called me and says, “Miles would like you to do a performance with him.” So I said, “Yeah, okay.” And by now, I mean that was like a couple of years later. By now I’m playing literally around the world with Keith Jarrett, Jack DeJohnette, and Charles Lloyd. And we are having a great time. That was just my joy. So Miles Davis, that was going to be just a gig. You know, in Buffalo, New York. So quite frankly, I had no idea of the immensity of that. Because I just wanted to play what we were playing. I

mean playing with Jack and Keith were just all I was about. But on 77th Street on the third floor of Miles’ brownstone we had gone through all the tunes, the music was like that — right? And no Miles Davis. Right? So at the conclusion of the rehearsal, the last tune in the Key of C there was Herbie and Wayne were at the piano discussing the voicing of a G something chord, a G 7 chord. And they couldn’t find it. All of a sudden burst through the door was Miles Davis. He went over to the piano and he said [whispers] “You play it like this.” And this thing is like a little, skinny, fingers are like little matchsticks. I mean, pencils. And he put his fingers on the piano very carefully and the sound was just wonderful. And I said to myself so he’s the guy that teaches all these guys what he, you know, needs harmonically and contextually. And so he didn’t say anything to me and walked right out. Didn’t even look at me, walked right out. So my first thought was this guy’s been standing outside listening to me. Right? So I said, oh okay. But apparently I did something right because I found myself on the gig for next week in Buffalo, New York. And the moment I hit the stage Miles put me through the heat man, he just, you know, man, he did everything opposite we rehearsed. Called all the tunes that we didn’t rehearse. And all fast tempos. So it was like, I felt like I was like against the wall — whap, whap, whap, whap. I said please, please.
Well he was a boxer, wasn’t he?
Well I wanted to hit him but he might knock me out. So I said well — that’s what happened. Not much fun but it was a good experience.
